preamble: Lowering and unrounding of the first element of [ui]/[ʊɪ]. In Early Modern English, the late Middle English diphthong /ʊɪ/ of boil, join, point and poison merged with /əɪ/~/aɪ/, the Great Vowel Shift reflex of Middle English /iː/, so that join rhymed with line. Standard English later restored /ɔɪ/ from regional variants, but forms like 'jine', 'pint' (point) and 'bile' (boil) survived in dialect speech.

examples.from: join, boil with late Middle English /ʊɪ/
examples.note: The merger is shown by late 17th- and early 18th-century rhymes: 'join–line' in Pope, 'Mind–join'd' in Congreve, 'toils–smiles' in Dryden.

sources: Wikipedia contributors. Line–loin merger (citing Barber, C. (1997). Early Modern English, pp. 108–116). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line%E2%80%93loin_merger
